openers.agri: Every field is a soil someone has decided to manage. This part of the course turns to agricultural soil science, the branch that studies soil conditions as they bear on growing food and fibre. It begins with the big choices a farmer makes: whether to bring water in, which crops to grow and in what order, and whether to rely on natural inputs such as compost and manure. Each choice leaves a mark. Water poured onto a field carries soluble nutrients away, and a single crop grown year after year wears the land in ways a sequence of crops does not.
openers.farming-systems-and-growing-media: Water is where farming systems start. People apply controlled amounts of it to land to grow crops, landscape plants and lawns, spreading it over the surface by gravity or spraying it overhead from high-pressure sprinklers. Yet only part of that water is ever used by the crop, and what drains away can take soluble plant nutrients with it. This chapter also follows the crops themselves, from a single crop grown year after year to a series of different ones, and the farms that rely on compost, manure and green manure. It ends with the land and the media plants grow in: new land won from seas and lake beds, and the potting mixes that hold plants in containers.

soil-agri-013.title: Irrigation: bringing water to the crop
soil-agri-013.text: In Khuzistan, in south-west Iran, farmers were steering water onto their fields in the 6th millennium BCE. Irrigation is the application of controlled amounts of water to land to help grow crops, landscape plants and lawns. Many cultures have practised it for over 5,000 years. The water comes from groundwater, rivers, lakes and reservoirs, or from treated wastewater, desalinated water, drainage water and even fog collection. Usually it tops up rainfall. Only in arid lands, or outside the rainy season in semi-arid areas, does it supply nearly all of a crop's water. It does other jobs too: it revegetates disturbed soils in dry areas, protects crops from frost, suppresses weeds in grain fields and prevents soil consolidation. The main methods are {{ref:soil-agri-049}}, the oldest; {{ref:soil-agri-016}}; micro-irrigation such as {{ref:soil-agri-015}}; and {{ref:soil-agri-017}}, which raises the water table. The scale is vast. Land equipped for irrigation reached 355 million ha in 2023, more than twice the 1960s area. That is 23% of croplands, and irrigated yields average 76% above rainfed ones. Getting the amount right matters. Over-irrigation raises water tables and causes irrigation salinity, which then needs subsurface drainage. Under-irrigation controls salinity poorly, so toxic salts build up at the surface. That is why drainage is so often studied with irrigation, and why the two are often needed together to sustain high crop production.

soil-agri-004.title: Crop rotation: a different crop each season
soil-agri-004.text: Between the 9th and 11th centuries, European farmers changed how they divided their fields, moving from two-field to three-field schemes. Crop rotation is growing a series of different crops on the same land over successive growing seasons. A later four-field sequence of wheat, turnips, barley and clover was key to the British Agricultural Revolution. Rotation works on several fronts. It lessens a crop's reliance on one set of nutrients, cuts pest and weed pressure, and lowers the chance that resistant pests and weeds develop. Plants of one family share pests and pathogens, so a rotation pays attention to plant family. Changing crops then breaks pest life cycles and habitats. Legumes such as alfalfa and clover hold nitrogen in root nodules. After harvest their leftover roots decay and release it to the next, nitrogen-demanding crop. A well-designed rotation can reduce the need for synthetic fertilizers and for weed killers, and it improves soil structure and organic matter, which reduces erosion. Rotations greatly increase the carbon held in soil organic matter, and long, highly diverse rotations do so most. Disturbing the soil by {{ref:soil-agri-095}} pulls the other way, driving an exponential decline. In Brazil, conversion to {{ref:soil-agri-117}} with intensive rotations stored carbon in the soil at 0.41 tonnes per hectare per year. Mistakes are slow to surface. A faulty rotation can unbalance soil nutrients or build up pathogens, and the damage may take years to show and as long to correct.

soil-agri-021.title: Leaching: when water carries nutrients away
soil-agri-021.text: Rain that soaks through a field does not leave empty-handed. In farming, leaching is the loss of water-soluble plant nutrients from soil, carried away by rain and irrigation water. It is the same downward washing described in {{ref:soil-form-050}}, seen from the farmer's side. Growers weigh soil structure, crop planting and the type and rate of fertilizer to avoid losing too much. The word has a second, deliberate meaning. Farmers sometimes apply a small excess of salty {{ref:soil-agri-013}} water so that salts do not build up, and this usually needs drainage to remove the extra water. Leaching becomes an environmental concern when seeping water carries dissolved chemicals into groundwater. On farms the main sources are excess fertilizer, poorly stored manure and biocides, the chemicals used to kill pests. The losses can cascade. Leaching of nitrate from acidic sources can increase losses of calcium and other soil nutrients, lowering an ecosystem's productivity. Areas with high rainfall become acidic through leaching. Among the measures used to reduce nutrient leaching are {{ref:soil-fert-050}}, a charcoal added to soil, and {{ref:soil-agri-068}}, sown to take up what is left behind.

soil-agri-040.title: Land reclamation: making new ground from water
soil-agri-040.text: Almost a sixth of the Netherlands, about 7,000 km2, was once sea, lake, marsh or swamp. Land reclamation is the creation of new land from oceans, seas, riverbeds or lake beds, and the result is called reclaimed land or land fill. Builders infill with heavy rock or cement topped with clay and dirt, drain submerged wetlands for farming, or dredge. The practice is old: Egypt's Twelfth Dynasty (c. 2000–1800 BC) made farmland around Lake Moeris by diverting its water with levees and canals. China has reclaimed more than 13,500 km2. New ground is fragile ground. It is highly susceptible to soil liquefaction in earthquakes, and consolidation of soft ground is a common technical risk. Fill compaction and drained {{ref:soil-water-144}} both cause subsidence, and drained marshes eventually sink below the surrounding water. Draining wetlands for ploughing also destroys habitat. Nearly 65% of the Yellow Sea's tidal flats have been reclaimed, and some countries now restrict new projects.

soil-agri-046.title: Herbicides, the chemistry of weed control
soil-agri-046.text: Between 1900 and 2000, yields of major crops per acre rose three to six times. Herbicides, substances commonly called weed killers and used to control unwanted plants, were part of that rise, together with nitrogen fertilizer and better cultivars. Selective herbicides control particular weeds and leave the crop largely unharmed. Non-selective ones kill plants indiscriminately. Before herbicides, farmers controlled weeds culturally, for example by changing soil pH, salinity or fertility. Major breakthroughs came during the Second World War. Glyphosate, marketed as Roundup from 1971, is now used very widely on crops bred to resist it. The costs are real. Herbicide use generally harms the environment, seriously damaging insects, non-target plants, animals and aquatic systems. Weeds can also evolve resistance, and switching between herbicides with different modes of action slows that selection. A well-designed {{ref:soil-agri-004}} can reduce herbicide needs, while {{ref:soil-agri-117}} may increase them.

soil-agri-001.title: Agricultural soil science: soil in the service of food
soil-agri-001.text: For most of its history, soil science was farm science. Agricultural soil science is the branch that studies soil conditions as they bear on growing food and fibre. Until pedology arose in the 19th century, it was the only branch, then known as {{ref:soil-found-097}}. It belongs to agronomy, so it is also called soil agronomy, and some regions know it as agrology. The field studies the chemical, physical, biological and mineralogical makeup of soils as they relate to farming, and it develops methods that raise food and fibre production. Its favourite variables read like a soil checklist: texture, aeration and porosity, drainage, water content and water potential, horizonation, fertility, soil biota, and pH with cation-exchange capacity. Its research covers irrigation and drainage, {{ref:soil-agri-095}}, soil classification, plant nutrition and soil fertility, and newer areas such as greenhouse effect mitigation. Soil husbandry, the careful keeping of soil, is a strong tradition within it. Old problems remain. Erosion, compaction, lowered fertility and contamination are still serious concerns, and the field puts growing emphasis on keeping soils productive in the long term. Pushing for maximum yield can carry high costs, such as massive crop diseases in monocultures or groundwater contaminated by fertilizers and pesticides.

soil-agri-028.title: Potting soil, which usually holds no soil
soil-agri-028.text: The bag says potting soil, but the contents are usually something else. Potting soil, also called growing medium or potting mix, is a substrate used to grow plants in containers. It holds little or no real soil, because soil compacts and loses pore space with repeated watering and is too heavy for pots. Instead come peat, vermiculite, {{ref:soil-agri-139}}, bark chips, perlite, sand, rice hulls and similar materials, usually mixing organic and inorganic ones. A typical recipe combines something to hold moisture, something for aeration and drainage, and fertilizer. A good medium holds water and nutrients, drains the excess, leaves pore space for root oxygen and decomposes slowly. Peat is usually limed to cut its acidity, typically 8.5 pounds of limestone per cubic yard (5.0 kg/m3). Peat is also controversial. Harvesting it degrades peatlands. They accumulate as little as 1 mm a year, yet they store up to 30% of the carbon held in soils on 3% of the world's surface. Commercial mixes are usually sterilized, and outbreaks of Legionnaires' disease have been traced to potting mix in several countries.

soil-agri-135.title: Organic farming: growing without synthetic inputs
soil-agri-135.text: By 2022, about 96 million hectares in 188 countries were farmed organically by 4.5 million farmers, about 2 percent of world farmland. Organic farming relies on natural inputs such as {{ref:soil-fert-028}}, manure and green manure, with techniques such as {{ref:soil-agri-004}} and mixed cropping. It aims at sustainability, soil fertility and biodiversity, and with rare exceptions it prohibits synthetic pesticides, synthetic fertilizers and genetically modified organisms. The movement arose in the early 20th century, partly because chemical farming brought soil compaction, erosion and declining fertility. Albert Howard, called the father of organic farming, adopted Northbourne's term in An Agricultural Testament in 1940. The trade-off is yield. A 2012 meta-analysis put organic productivity on average 25% below conventional, and a 2011 analysis found organic yields averaged 80% of conventional. That gap reshapes the environmental sums. Nitrogen leaching and nitrous oxide emissions are lower per area but higher per amount of food. Lower yields can also push more land into farming, which may cause biodiversity loss and negative climate effects.

soil-agri-049.title: Surface irrigation: letting gravity spread the water
soil-agri-049.text: In many places, farmers water their fields almost exactly as their ancestors did thousands of years ago. Surface irrigation spreads water over the soil surface by gravity, and it is by far the most common form of irrigation worldwide. It is often called flood irrigation, a name implying uncontrolled, inefficient distribution. Some forms, such as surge irrigation, are in fact closely managed. Each irrigation runs in four phases: advance, storage, depletion and recession. The depth soaking in at any point depends on the opportunity time, the time water stands on the surface there. Border strip irrigation, a hybrid of basin and furrow methods, runs water down long, narrow bays between earth banks, often for dairy pasture. Too much water causes waterlogging and deep drainage, and rising water tables can lift salt from saline layers into the root zone. Yet surface irrigation's relatively high leaching fraction makes salinization less of a problem than with other methods, unless poor subsurface drainage blocks the salt from leaching. Long use leaves its own soil, a recognisable irragric {{ref:soil-class-120}}.

soil-agri-053.title: Monocropping: the same crop, year after year
soil-agri-053.text: Between 1845 and 1849, one opportunistic species destroyed Ireland's potatoes and brought the Great Famine. A single cultivar with one resistance strategy is that exposed. Monocropping, also called continuous cropping, is growing a single crop year after year on the same land. Maize, soybeans and wheat are often grown this way, because a farmer can then use the same seed, pest control and machinery across the farm. The soil pays. Repeating one crop depletes certain nutrients and breeds pests and weeds adapted to it, so the system leans harder on pesticides and artificial fertilizers. Those chemicals seeping into soil and groundwater are a well-known concern. Monocropping also aids soil erosion, which mixed cropping and {{ref:soil-agri-004}} significantly reduce. Whether it is worth it remains disputed. Advocates say growing many crops together would be costly and could not feed everyone. Critics reject this, citing monocropping's damage to societies and the environment.

soil-agri-014.title: Irrigation efficiency: how much water the crop really uses
soil-agri-014.text: On many farms, 40% to 60% of irrigation water is lost before a crop can use it. Irrigation efficiency is the share of applied water the crop actually uses: the water it transpires divided by the water applied, times 100. The excess seeps away or runs off, carrying nutrients or pesticides with it. Sprinkler, drip or well-managed surface systems can reach 70% or more. Better design and better scheduling raise efficiency, and with it the crop grown per unit of water.

soil-agri-016.title: Sprinkler irrigation: rain on demand
soil-agri-016.text: Sprinkler irrigation pipes water to points in the field and sprays it overhead from high-pressure sprinklers or guns. In centre pivot systems the sprinklers ride on wheeled towers that circle around a central water feed, and they can irrigate all types of terrain. Newer pivots hang drop heads just above the crop, or drag hoses that wet the ground directly, to limit evaporation. This is Low Energy Precision Application, or LEPA. Using sprinkler and micro-irrigation lowers the risk of waterlogging and erosion. One hazard is the water itself: salty sprinkler water can burn leaves even where the soil is not saline.

soil-agri-017.title: Subirrigation: watering plants from below
soil-agri-017.text: Some crops are watered without a drop falling on the surface. Subirrigation artificially raises the water table so that the soil is moistened from below the plants' root zone. Farmers have long used it for field crops where water tables are high, often on lowland or river-valley grassland, setting ditch levels with pumps, canals, weirs and gates. In greenhouses a nutrient solution floods potted plants from below for 10–20 minutes and is then pumped back for reuse, saving water and nutrients. Self-watering containers and wicking beds work the same way on a small scale, drawing water up from a reservoir by capillary action.

soil-agri-018.title: Wastewater irrigation: watering crops with city sewage
soil-agri-018.text: Wastewater irrigation waters crops with recycled or untreated municipal wastewater. Its nitrogen and phosphorus act as fertilizer. The supply is cheaper than some sources, and it keeps flowing whatever the season or water restrictions. Developing countries increasingly use untreated wastewater, often unsafely. The hazards include bacteria, heavy metals, pharmaceuticals and pesticides, and their effects depend on both the wastewater and the soil. WHO's 2006 guidelines advise a multiple-barrier approach, such as stopping irrigation a few days before harvest so that pathogens die off.

soil-agri-044.title: Fallow: giving a field a season off
soil-agri-044.text: Under a two-field rotation, half the land lay idle each year. Leaving cropland unsown for one or more growing cycles is called fallow. A fallow field recovers and stores organic matter while keeping its moisture. Removing the crop also removes the hosts of pests and soil-borne pathogens, breaking their cycles. Intensive farming has shrunk fallow land, along with field margins and hedges, often by sowing {{ref:soil-agri-066}} instead. Rest carries a risk. A field can be most vulnerable to erosion while fallow, so keeping stubble cover, for example by {{ref:soil-agri-117}}, is key to reducing soil loss. Covered ground also holds more life: those crops raised microbial biomass carbon by about 20% and particulate organic carbon by nearly 50% compared with bare or fallow ground. An improved fallow enhances the rest period, for example by sowing yellow sweetclover, under which weeds made up only 1–12% of standing biomass.

soil-agri-042.title: Regenerative agriculture: farming to rebuild topsoil
soil-agri-042.text: Since farmers began turning the soil, an estimated 30–75% of global soil organic matter has been lost. Regenerative agriculture is a conservation and rehabilitation approach to farming that aims to regenerate {{ref:soil-form-021}}, raise biodiversity and strengthen the health of farm soil. It is not one practice but a mix: little or no turning of the soil, {{ref:soil-agri-066}}, crop rotations, compost and grazing. The Rodale Institute began using the term in the early 1980s. Pinning it down is hard. A 2020 review of 229 articles found no legal or widely accepted definition. The evidence is mixed too. A 2023 review found that several of its practices can improve the soil's carbon, its health or yields under some climates and soils. Results vary between farming systems. Its climate claims are disputed. Scientists have criticized claims that it can mitigate climate change by locking carbon in soil as exaggerated and unsupported by evidence.

soil-agri-007.title: Choosing the crops in a rotation
soil-agri-007.text: Every crop in a rotation either gives the field something or takes something away. Choosing them means weighing organic matter, nutrients, pest control and protection from erosion. Row crops such as vegetables often pay best but tax the soil: low biomass and shallow roots leave little residue. Grasses and cereals, with dense, far-reaching roots, build structure and organic matter and compete with weeds. Two rules follow. A nitrogen-fixing legume should precede a nitrogen-depleting crop, and a low-residue crop should be offset by a high-biomass {{ref:soil-agri-066}}.

soil-agri-006.title: Rotations that hold soil in place
soil-agri-006.text: In a decade-long study, fall rye sown after the potato harvest cut soil run-off by as much as 43%. Rotations can be built to fight erosion through crop sequences and the management of residue and fallow, often alongside {{ref:soil-agri-117}}. Protection is greatest when the most crop stubble stays on the surface, slowing overland flow and its power to carry sediment. Decomposing forage crops glue particles into aggregates that resist raindrops, running water and wind. Where rain is unpredictable, sowing only when soil water is adequate gives better cover than a rigid rotation.

soil-agri-008.title: Mixed farming: crops and livestock on one farm
soil-agri-008.text: On a mixed farm, crops and animals feed each other. Mixed farming combines growing crops with keeping livestock, which helps manage rotations and cycle nutrients. The animals eat what is left of the crops after harvest, and their manure replenishes crop nutrients. Nutrients thus cycle within the farm, and less synthetic fertilizer is needed. Livestock make efficient use of sod and of crops sown to cover the ground, spreading their nutrients as manure instead of exporting them as sold hay. Regenerative grazing of ruminants on such farms has improved nutrient cycling by speeding the decomposition of crop leftovers.

soil-agri-009.title: Polyculture: several crops in one place
soil-agri-009.text: The Three Sisters plant corn with pole beans and squash. The beans supply nitrogen, and the squash spreads a canopy that suppresses weeds. Polyculture is growing two or more crops in the same place at the same time, the opposite of {{ref:soil-agri-053}}. {{ref:soil-agri-133}} and companion planting add diversity within one season. Double-cropping grows two crops in sequence in one season, or a crop alongside a ground-covering crop. This suits small farms that cannot rest land for long. Rotations work for both single crops and mixtures, so farmers can raise biodiversity in space and in time.

soil-agri-133.title: Intercropping: sharing a field to harvest more
soil-agri-133.text: Two crops in one field can yield more than either would alone. Intercropping, a form of polyculture, grows two or more crops at the same time in the same field. The goal is usually a greater yield, by using resources or ecological processes a single crop would leave unused. Crops are chosen so they do not compete for space, nutrients, water or light, for example a deep-rooted crop with a shallow-rooted one. In mixed intercropping the crops are freely mixed. Temporal intercropping pairs a fast-growing crop with a slow-growing one. Relay cropping sows the second crop while the first is still growing. Rotation does not count, because its crops grow in separate seasons. In low-input or subsistence farming, intercropping can give higher yields for the same input. Pest control by trap crops has had mixed success: of 100 examples reviewed in 2006, only 10 succeeded commercially.
